endorsements.quote: For example, a chatbot providing advice to patients about CKD management should have its answers measured against established clinical guidelines and/or experienced nephrologist responses.

Clinicians must remain diligent when checking the outputs of AI, e.g., by proof-reading AI-generated reports or correspondence, and avoid overreliance on its outputs (so-called automation bias), particularly when they do not match the broader context of the patient's clinical picture.
To overcome these bias related concerns, there must be a deliberate search for sources of bias to address them before implementation of any AI system.
Data used to train the AI model must be representative of the population it is to be used in, including being reflective of ethnicity and gender distribution.

Administrators must also be mindful of the shortcomings of AI particularly for ethical distribution of care and undertake regular fairness audits to identify technology i.e., inadvertently promoting disadvantage.

Beyond legal regulation, AI developers can integrate privacy safeguards into their systems by minimizing data collection, using encryption, restricting access to authorized users, and establishing clear data retention and deletion protocols.
Nephrologists must also have enough knowledge about any AI tool they intend to use to adequately explain its function and associated risks to their patients.

This highlights a clear educational need for current certified nephrologists, ideally through hospital employers or professional bodies, to ensure they have the knowledge to use AI safely and explain it clearly to patients.

Clinicians should also be aware of any local laws obligating disclosure and consent for AI use in clinical encounters, e.g., surveillance laws affecting use of ambient digital scribes in some US states and Australia.
To address this, there must also be explicit consideration of human oversight requirements for any consequential AI program, together with clear accountability chains for errors.
Therefore, when contemplating development and particularly deployment of AI technologies, environmental effects should form a key consideration.
Include equity in AI procurement decisions

unlisted_practices: Rigorously test AI tools before implementation in the population of intended use.
Establish clear audit requirements for routine evaluation of AI outputs, especially for models that evolve with new data.
Increase human oversight of AI used in resource allocation decisions such as transplant allocation, and consider limiting AI use in some high-stakes settings.
Place primary responsibility for ensuring AI accuracy with health care institutions and regulatory bodies rather than individual clinicians.
Do not upload sensitive clinical information to external or unverified AI platforms.
Advocate for funding and infrastructure to develop AI tools for resource-constrained settings.
Identify patient populations at risk of being unable to access AI-related tools.
Include environmental effect in AI procurement decisions.
Approach black box AI results with special caution and emphasize clinician oversight.
